newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. rethinking stalled Western Sahara operation.
newsitem.headline: U.N. rethinking stalled Western Sahara operation.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Friday he was studying whether a long-stalled U.N. peace plan for the disupted territory of Western Sahara could still be carried out, or whether it could be modified or some different solution found.

He was referring, in a report to the Security Council, to a plan that called for a U.N.-organised referendum in January 1992 to decide whether the former Spanish colony should be incorporated into Morocco, which controls most of the territory, or become independent, as called for by the Polisario Front.

A brushfire war was largely halted by a ceasefire in September 1991, monitored by a U.N. observer force. But continuing differences between the two sides over who should be allowed to vote in the referendum resulted in repeated postponements. Voter identification has been stalled since late 1995.

"In the circumstances, I believe it essential to make every effort to move the political process forward and to identify ways, including the possibility of a new initiative, to overcome the current stalemate in implementing the settlement plan," Annan wrote.
"I have therefore been reviewing the following questions:
A. Can the settlement plan be implemented in its
B. If not, are there adjustments to the settlement
plan, acceptable to both parties, which would make it implementable?
C. If not, are there other ways by which the
international community could help the parties resolve their conflict?"

Annan said he intended intensifying the examination of those questions and to present conclusions to the Security Council before the May 31 expiry of the current mandate of the U.N. operation, called the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO).

He also said he was considering further reductions in the force, which was cut 20 percent last year and now includes 230 military observers and support personnel and nine civilian police, in addition to U.N. civilian staff.
Costs had already fallen by some 40 percent, from about $4 million a month to approximately $2.6 million, he added.

The withdrawal of the civilian police, if accompanied by additional reductions elsewhere, would allow further cuts in civilian administration staff, Annan said, promising to review the situation and inform the council.

"The international community cannot continue to spend its scarce resources on the Western Sahara in the absence of any progress in the implementation of the plan that the two parties freely accepted nine years ago," he said, referring to the origins of the proposed referendum
"This is a critical moment for the mission. I can only hope that the parties do not fail to realise the serious implications for the future of MINURSO."
